name: factory-method
intent: Define one creation operation whose declared result type is the product interface, and let whoever supplies that operation - a subclass override, an injected creator function, or a registry entry - decide which concrete class is instantiated, so client code binds only to the product interface and adding a product type never edits the code that uses it.
problem: A framework, base class or shared service must create objects whose concrete class it cannot know - the class depends on configuration, the runtime environment, a file header, the deployment, or data available only at execution time - so hard-coding the constructor in the shared code forces an edit of that shared code for every new variation.
context: Applies wherever a program part must produce objects of a type that varies per deployment, per configuration, per subclass or per input: framework extension points whose base class composes products it does not name, plugin/format/driver selection from runtime data, and test seams where the created collaborator must be substitutable. It is a construction-time decision, so it shapes the design only where creation is a genuine axis of variation.
benefits: Client code names only the product interface: new product types arrive without editing the code that uses them (GoF's open/closed consequence, 'eliminates the need to bind application-specific classes into your code').

Gives subclasses a hook: a framework or base class can let its extension supply an extended version of a composed object by overriding a single creation operation instead of re-implementing the whole algorithm.
Connects parallel class hierarchies: the creator hierarchy can mirror a product hierarchy without hard-wiring concrete classes together.
Creation can reuse instead of allocate: a factory method may return a cached, pooled or interned instance or a subclass instance - something a constructor is not allowed to do.
Localizes the knowledge of which class is built in one operation, giving it a name (of, fromIso, makeShape) that reads better than a bare constructor call and can validate before construction.
Creates a substitution seam: the creation step can be swapped in tests (creator function value, registry entry, DI registration) without touching call sites.
Enables policy injection at creation time: factories can wrap products with cross-cutting concerns (retry, timeout, telemetry, circuit breakers) at construction, keeping call sites clean.
Supports progressive complexity: a simple factory method scales from one hardcoded product to a registry to a full DI container without changing the product interface.
tradeoffs: Subclass explosion: a client that only wants a different product may have to subclass the Creator, adding a new point of evolution - the GoF's own stated disadvantage; if the caller has no other reason to be a subclass, composition or injection is cheaper.

Indirection cost per creation: a virtual call, a type-erased std::function/Swift existential/boxed trait object, or a map lookup, plus an extra allocation and lost inlining on the hot path; negligible next to real construction work, visible for tiny short-lived objects.

Ownership must be transferred explicitly: the factory returns a polymorphic object whose lifetime the caller now owns (unique_ptr, Box, Dispose), and a factory that caches instances must decide shared-versus-fresh and synchronize that decision.

The product key is resolved at run time, so a typo, a missing provider or a stale configuration is a run-time failure the compiler cannot see; the factory must define a failure mode (exception, Result, Option, null) and callers must handle it.

Comprehension and debugging cost: the class actually constructed is no longer visible at the call site, so readers and stack traces must follow the factory; the indirection is only worth it where the variation is real.

Construction-order hazard: an overridable factory method must not be called from the Creator's constructor, because the concrete override is not available while the base object is still being initialized (GoF's C++ note; the same rule applies to virtual calls in constructors generally).

participants.responsibility: Declares the interface of the objects the factory method creates; all clients and the creator itself see products only through it.
Implements the Product interface for one concrete class; reached only through the factory, never named by clients.
Declares the factory method (abstract or with a default product), holds the creation step as its extension point, and uses the returned Product in its own algorithm.
Overrides the factory method to return the appropriate ConcreteProduct (or reused instance) for its variant.

When no subclass exists, a first-class creator function, a Supplier/Func value or a registry entry keyed by product name carries the same decision; the factory is then a plain function or a container registration rather than an overridden method.

use_cases: Framework extension points: a base class (document/application, dialog/toolkit, parser) composes products it does not name and lets each subclass supply the concrete product via one overridden creation operation.
Runtime format or implementation selection from data: a decoder/driver/transport chosen by file magic, extension, media type or configuration (image decoders, JDBC drivers, codecs, storage backends).

Plugin and provider discovery: implementations registered under an id and resolved at startup, so the host compiles without knowing the plugin (Java ServiceLoader, Qt QCanBusFactory plugin system, .NET MEF).
Test seams: the production factory builds the real collaborator while a test substitutes a double, in-memory store or fake clock by swapping the creator - not the call sites.
Reuse-oriented creation: hand out an interned, pooled or already-configured instance where allocating a fresh object would be wrong or wasteful.
Parallel hierarchies: a toolkit/family whose creators pair one-to-one with the products they build, so both can be extended together.

JUnit 5 @TestFactory: dynamic test generation where a factory method computes test cases at runtime (from data tables, external files, or property-based inputs) and returns DynamicTest/DynamicContainer instances, decoupling test generation from static test class structure.

JDBC DriverManager / DataSource: DriverManager.getConnection(url, ...) selects a registered JDBC driver from the URL scheme; DataSource.getConnection() is a factory method on the JDBC abstraction that lets container frameworks (Spring, Jakarta EE) inject the correct driver without application code naming it.

Qt CAN bus plugins: QCanBusFactoryV2.createDevice() is a factory method that each Qt bus plugin (socketcan, peak, etc.) overrides to instantiate its device-specific QCanBusDevice subclass, decoupling the transport from the protocol handling layers.

Spring DI with Map-based factory: PaymentGatewayFactory(List<PaymentGateway> gateways) uses constructor injection of all registered gateways, builds a Map keyed by gateway.getType(), and selects the correct implementation at runtime — Spring automatically assembles the collection, turning the factory into a zero-configuration extension point.

AI/LLM provider routing: factory methods select which AI provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, local model) to use based on configuration, feature flags, or cost constraints, allowing the application to remain provider-agnostic at the call site.

Feature-flagged product selection: products are instantiated based on runtime feature flags (e.g., newrecommendation-engine-v2 vs legacy) enabling progressive rollouts and A/B testing without code changes.

Cross-region or multi-tenant routing: factories select backend implementations (database shards, storage adapters, telemetry exporters) based on tenant ID, region code, or compliance requirements at runtime.
Connection pool and resource management: factory returns pooled connections, cached HTTP clients, or reentrant locks where construction is expensive and reuse is semantically safe.

Protocol and codec negotiation: factories select serialization formats (JSON, Protobuf, Avro), compression algorithms, or network protocols based on client capabilities or configuration, decoupling protocol knowledge from business logic.

JDK static factory methods as creation seams: java.util.Calendar.getInstance(timeZone, locale) hands back whichever Calendar subclass the locale demands (Gregorian, JapaneseImperial, ...) and java.util.EnumSet.noneOf(type) picks RegularEnumSet for enums with at most 64 constants and JumboEnumSet beyond that - callers type against the abstract supertype and never name the concrete class.

factory_boy test fixtures (Python): each Factory subclass declares its product with class Meta: model = ..., create()/build() act as the creator's factory method, and a child factory such as AdminFactory(UserFactory) overrides which class and defaults are produced - the Creator/ConcreteCreator structure as a test-data extension point.
avoid_when: The concrete type never varies, or varies only with a compile-time constant: call the constructor (or a named constructor) directly - a factory with one branch is pure indirection.

The choice is a one-off wiring decision made at startup: pass the already-built collaborator, or register it in the composition root/dependency injection container, instead of building a creator hierarchy.
Construction is a multi-step assembly with optional parts: use Builder (or a type-safe builder) so the steps are ordered and validated.
You must create consistent families of related products: that is Abstract Factory, not one factory method per product; and cloning an already configured instance is Prototype.
The variation is about which algorithm runs on data that already exists: use Strategy - there is no creation decision to encapsulate.
The object is a small immutable value with no behaviour to hide: direct construction keeps the code readable and lets the compiler check the type.

You only need to vary object construction parameters but not the type itself: prefer a simple parameterized constructor or a configuration object; a factory is overkill when the interface never changes.
anti_patterns: Subclassing the Creator for every product when nothing else varies: a hierarchy of one-line creators that only exists to satisfy the pattern.
Static factory methods that merely forward the same parameter list to a constructor, adding an indirection layer (and hiding allocation and ownership) without any run-time choice.
Returning null/None/undefined for an unknown product key and letting the caller fail much later, instead of a defined error at the factory.
A global mutable registry that every module writes to implicitly: hidden process-wide state, order-dependent initialization and test leakage.
Leaving the concrete class names scattered in client code (or in an if-chain inside business logic) while claiming the factory encapsulates creation - the coupling moved, it did not disappear.
A factory that silently swallows construction failures (empty catch, default instance) so a misconfiguration looks like a working system.
A giant conditional inside a single mega-factory with dozens of branches instead of a registry or selector pattern — hard to maintain and test exhaustively.
A factory that returns concrete types instead of the product interface, re-introducing the coupling the pattern was meant to eliminate.
Over-engineering a factory where only one product exists and no variation is anticipated — adds indirection without benefit.
Using raw strings as factory keys without validation or enums — typos become runtime failures with no compile-time safety.
A factory with hidden side effects (network calls, file I/O, global state mutations) that make it unpredictable and hard to test in isolation.
Mixing business rules into the factory: if the factory also enforces pricing, eligibility, or compliance logic, it violates single responsibility and becomes hard to test and evolve.
design_principles: Open/closed principle: new product types are added by adding a creator, not by editing the clients that use the product interface.
Dependency inversion / program to an interface, not an implementation: clients and creators depend on the Product abstraction, and the concrete class is named in exactly one place.
Single responsibility: the decision of which class to build is separated from the code that uses the built object.
Encapsulate what varies: the construction detail is the axis of variation, so it gets its own operation.
Inversion of control: for frameworks, the base class calls the subclass's creation step (the Hollywood principle) rather than the subclass wiring its products into the base.
Interface segregation: keep the product interface narrow — clients should only depend on the operations they actually use, reducing the burden on each implementation.
Fail fast: detect and report construction failures at the factory boundary rather than allowing malformed objects to propagate through the system.
best_practices: Return the product interface (or an unexported/abstract type), never the concrete class, so no caller can depend on what the factory actually built.
Keep every concrete class name in exactly one place - the factory, registry or DI registration - and make that place the documented extension point.
Define and test the failure mode for an unknown or unsatisfiable key (exception, Result/Either, Option/optional, or an explicit error value); never return a half-constructed object.
Transfer ownership explicitly and document whether the factory allocates fresh instances or may reuse cached ones (unique_ptr/Box/Dispose, or a note that the returned instance is shared).
Prefer a creator function value or a container registration over a Creator subclass whenever callers have no other reason to subclass; keep the classic virtual creator for framework hooks.
Make factories thread-safe by construction: an immutable registry built at startup beats a mutable map that modules register into at arbitrary times.
Never call an overridable factory method from a constructor; let the base initialize the reference and create the product on first use (lazy initialization) instead.
Prefer enum keys or typed selectors over raw strings for product keys to catch typos at compile time rather than runtime; if strings are required, validate against a controlled vocabulary.
Keep product interfaces narrow: a bloated abstraction forces every implementation to support behaviour it does not need, increasing coupling and implementation cost.

Use dependency injection to supply factory dependencies (database pools, HTTP clients, configuration) rather than having the factory reach into global state; a factory that reads implicit global state is hard to test.

Test factory behaviour independently: verify that supported keys return the correct product type, unsupported keys raise the defined failure, and the lifecycle contract (fresh vs cached) matches the documentation.

When combining factory method with a DI container, let the container resolve the factory's stable dependencies while the factory method handles runtime variant selection — the container owns the object graph, the factory owns the variant.
Instrument factories with telemetry (creation counts, latency, error rates) to detect configuration drift, missing providers, or memory leaks from cached objects.

Document and enforce lifecycle semantics explicitly: is the returned object fresh (caller owns), shared (caller shares with pool), or scoped (bound to a context)? Inconsistent lifecycle is a source of subtle bugs.

Prefer composition over inheritance for factory variants: a registry of creator functions is more flexible and easier to test than a Creator subclass hierarchy for variants that differ only in which product they return.

Consider architecture tests (e.g., ArchUnit, DeprecationWarnings, import restrictions) to enforce that product implementations are only constructed through factory interfaces, not directly in application code.

When factories produce objects that hold resources (connections, handles, file descriptors), ensure the factory or the returned product implements proper cleanup (disposable/auto-closeable) and document who is responsible for lifetime management.
For expensive-to-construct products, make initialization explicit (e.g., separate warmup() call) rather than paying the cost on every creation — this prevents surprising latency spikes in production.

Validate inputs at the factory boundary before constructing: a factory is the choke point where invalid configurations should fail fast with clear error messages, not deep inside product construction.

When combining Factory Method with feature flags or progressive rollouts, ensure the factory's product selection is deterministic and auditable — log which product was selected and why, so production issues can be traced back to configuration.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Factory Method, Creational Patterns chapter, pp. 107-116 (also known as Virtual Constructor).

Joshua Bloch, Effective Java, 3rd Edition (2018), Item 1: 'Consider static factory methods instead of constructors' — distinguishes static factory idiom from GoF Factory Method, covers valueOf/getInstance/newInstance naming conventions, instance-controlled classes, and the service provider framework foundation (JDBC DriverManager).

Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2003), Plugin pattern (https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/plugin.html) — describes runtime service provider selection via factory methods as the bridge between Separated Interface and runtime configuration; Inversion of Control Containers article (https://martinfowler.com/articles/injection.html) connects factory methods to dependency injection.

Andrei Alexandrescu, Modern C++ Design: Generic Programming and Design Patterns Applied (2001), Chapter 8 'Object Factories' — provides template-based generic factory with TypeMap, FactoryError policy, and clone factories; states object factories are 'a cornerstone of virtually any quality polymorphic design'.

Google Research, 'Better Construction with Factories' (https://research.google/pubs/better-construction-with-factories/) — proposes factories as a separate layer in object construction to decouple client code from specific constructors, covering factories as class services alongside methods and constructors.

Ellis & Stroul, 'The Factory Pattern in API Design: A Usability Evaluation' (CMU, 2007, https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~marmalade/papers/Ellis2007FactoryUsability.pdf) — evaluates Abstract Factory and Factory Method from a usability perspective, finding that explicit downcasting and factory complexity are liabilities in API design.

Alexandrescu & modern parameterized factory implementation (JOT FM, 2010, https://www.jot.fm/issues/issue_2010_01/column5.pdf) — modern compact implementation using static factory methods and reflection to avoid separate Factory subclass proliferation.

Refactoring.Guru, Factory Method pattern (https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/factory-method) — comprehensive modern treatment with decision matrix, code examples in multiple languages, and visual structure diagrams.

Software Patterns Lexicon, Java Factory Patterns in JDBC Connection APIs (https://softwarepatternslexicon.com/java/design-patterns-in-java-standard-libraries/factory-patterns-in-jdbc/) — treats JDBC DriverManager and DataSource as primary real-world Factory Method examples in Java standard libraries.

TheLinuxCode, 'Factory Method Design Pattern: A Practical Guide for Evolving Systems' (https://thelinuxcode.com/factory-method-design-pattern-a-practical-guide-for-evolving-systems/) — covers production considerations: lifecycle hooks, cross-cutting concerns at creation, thread safety, observability, feature-flagged product selection, and architecture tests.

TheCodeForge, 'Factory Pattern in Java Explained' (https://thecodeforge.io/java/factory-pattern-java/) — practical guidance on enum keys, instance vs static factories, exhaustiveness, and when to introduce a factory.

Thinking in Python, Factory Patterns (https://thinkinginpython.com/27_Patterns--Factory.html) — compares Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, and Prototype with guidance on when to use each based on intent and structure.
C2 Wiki, 'Factory Pattern Considered Harmful' (https://wiki.c2.com/) — documents common pitfalls and over-engineering risks when applying factory patterns indiscriminately.

Harness.io, 'Simplify Test Maintenance with the Builder Factory Pattern' (https://www.harness.io/blog/builder-factory-pattern-testing) — describes using a Factory that produces pre-configured builders for test setup, reducing boilerplate and centralizing default object creation for test maintenance.

Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Factory Method section reproduced online (https://www.cs.unc.edu/~stotts/GOF/hires/pat3c.htm) — accessible copy of the canonical text: 'Define an interface for creating an object, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate', the abstract-Creator vs concrete-Creator variants, and the do-not-call-from-constructor warning.

Wikipedia, 'Factory method pattern' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factory_method_pattern) — canonical overview with worked examples (MazeGame.makeRoom overridden per game variant) and the FactoryMaker variant where a class-level factory method selects among concrete factories.

Oracle, java.util.Calendar API documentation (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java.util.Calendar.html) — getInstance() overloads as a real factory method: the returned Calendar subclass is chosen from the supplied TimeZone/Locale and never named to callers.

Oracle, java.util.EnumSet API documentation (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java.util.EnumSet.html) — the noneOf(Class) factory selects the compact RegularEnumSet representation for enums with up to 64 constants and JumboEnumSet otherwise; the product class is a hidden implementation detail.

Mark Seemann, 'Factory Overload' (https://blog.ploeh.dk/2011-12-19/FactoryOverload/) — misuse analysis: a factory layer becomes a leaky abstraction when call sites never actually vary, arguing for direct construction and narrow factory interfaces.

Factory Boy documentation, 'Introduction' (https://factoryboy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/introduction.html) — Python fixtures library whose Factory subclasses with class Meta: model = ... implement the Creator/ConcreteCreator structure for test-data generation.

related_patterns_notes.abstract-factory: Abstract Factory extends Factory Method by providing a family of related product creation methods in a single interface, ensuring products from the same family are used together. Where Factory Method has one creation operation per product type, Abstract Factory has one per product family. Factory Method is often the implementation mechanism for an Abstract Factory's creation methods; distinction: Use Factory Method when only the type of a single product varies; use Abstract Factory when families of related products must vary together consistently.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: Factory Method is structurally a special case of Template Method: the creator's algorithm calls the factory method just as any template method calls its primitive operation. The GoF explicitly notes that Factory Method is a template method applied to object creation. Both patterns defer a step to a subclass, but Template Method defers an algorithmic step while Factory Method defers object instantiation; distinction: Use Factory Method when the variation is which object is created; use Template Method when the variation is which algorithm steps are performed.
related_patterns_notes.prototype: Both patterns defer the decision of which concrete class to instantiate. Prototype clones a pre-configured instance (the prototype) instead of naming its class directly. A Prototype registry is functionally similar to a Factory Method registry, but creation is by copying rather than construction. Prototype avoids class explosion when products are complex to configure but easy to copy; distinction: Use Factory Method when construction logic is the variation; use Prototype when the variation is the pre-configured state of the instance and copying is cheaper than construction.
related_patterns_notes.builder: Builder and Factory Method both encapsulate object creation, but Builder handles multi-step construction with optional or ordered parameters, while Factory Method handles single-step type selection. A Builder is often passed to a Factory Method so the factory can invoke builder steps to construct the product. Conversely, a Builder may use a Factory Method internally to obtain initial product instances to configure; distinction: Use Factory Method for single-step type selection; use Builder when construction involves multiple steps, optional parameters, or ordered assembly that needs validation.
related_patterns_notes.named-constructor: Named Constructor is a related idiom (not a full GoF pattern) that addresses the same problem of readability and overloading ambiguity that Factory Method solves. A named constructor is a static factory method returning a fully constructed instance of the defining class — the class is known, only the construction signature varies. Factory Method extends this by making the class itself unknown; distinction: Use Named Constructor when the type is known but construction signatures are ambiguous or need validation; use Factory Method when the concrete type itself is the variation.
related_patterns_notes.dependency-injection: Dependency Injection is a broader composition principle that can use Factory Method as its creation mechanism. A DI container or container-managed factory creates and injects dependencies; the container often uses factory-method-like semantics to resolve which implementation to instantiate. Factory Method and DI are complementary: Factory Method is a pattern for the factory itself, while DI is a pattern for how the factory is supplied to clients; distinction: Use Factory Method for the internal creation logic; use DI to supply that factory (or its products) to clients without them needing to know which factory created the object.
related_patterns_notes.factory: Factory (sometimes called Simple Factory) is an informal pattern where a single class or function decides which concrete class to instantiate based on a parameter. Factory Method formalizes this by moving the decision to a subclass or a configurable registry. Simple Factory is often a stepping stone; Factory Method is the refactored result when the factory itself needs to be extended or mocked; distinction: Use Simple Factory for one-off type selection; use Factory Method when the creation decision itself needs to be substitutable, extensible, or mockable.
related_patterns_notes.functional-options: Functional Options is a pattern (particularly in Go, but applicable elsewhere) where configuration is passed as options closures rather than parameters. It can complement Factory Method when the factory needs to accept flexible configuration without requiring a separate Builder. The factory accepts a variadic list of Option[T] functions that configure the product before returning it; distinction: Use Factory Method for type selection; use Functional Options when the variation is in how the selected type is configured, not which type is selected.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Both Strategy and Factory Method involve selecting an implementation at runtime, but Strategy selects an algorithm to perform on data that already exists, while Factory Method selects which object to create. A Strategy is often used inside a product created by a Factory Method; distinction: Use Strategy when the variation is which algorithm runs on existing data; use Factory Method when the variation is which object is constructed.
related_patterns_notes.registry: A registry (often a map from string/enum to creator function) is a common implementation of Factory Method's modern functional form. The registry decouples product implementations from the factory interface and allows plugins or extensions to register themselves without modifying the core factory code; distinction: A registry is a specific implementation technique for Factory Method; they are often used together, with the registry providing the lookup mechanism for the factory's creation decision.
